## How This Page Works {#how}

Each year shows the government on 1 July.

In power means that a populist leads the government or is a partner in it. A party that supports a government from outside is shown, and not counted as in power.

There are two views, and you can choose. Either view shows the stronger of the two.

Parties in government come from PPEG, and The PopuList says which of them are populist. The two are linked through the IDs of Party Facts. In a few places an ID was missing or pointed to another party. There the link was made by hand, the reason was written down, and the party is marked "linked by Populi*Verse*". [The list of these links](#links) stands under the page's charts and can be downloaded. This view covers The PopuList's 31 European countries.

Heads of government come from the Global Populism Database, which grades their speeches. A term with an average of 0.5 or more counts as populist. In the words of its paper, Hawkins et al. 2019, that is somewhat populist or above. A leader counts only where he or she heads the government. In PPEG's countries that is the person PPEG names for the cabinet, or the president where the cabinet is presidential. Elsewhere it is the leader the database holds. A president beside a prime minister is shown in the country's panel and not counted.

Striped means a borderline case. The PopuList calls some parties borderline populist in some years. Where a country's place rests on such a party alone, the map and the chart show it striped.

Not known means that a party in the government has no Party Facts ID and no checked link, so it cannot be looked up.

Hatched means not covered. It never means none. The datasets end at different years. PPEG holds governments to 31 October 2025. The Global Populism Database grades a leader only for the terms it has coded, and for many countries its last term ended years ago. For the United States, for example, its last graded term is that of Donald Trump from 2017 to 2021. The map shows a year only where a dataset holds it. A country says why it is not covered when you point at it or open it.

Today comes from the Monitor. It shows only the actors on the Monitor's list, each with the source that classes it, and whether they hold power as of its latest issue. An actor is on the list because a dataset or a study classed it at some time. For a leader, the page names the terms whose speeches were graded. Now is therefore not a new grading. A country without an actor is not a country without populists in power.
